title: String Formatter Functions
story: Your school club wants a louder announcement for the hallway screen. You'll build small string-formatter functions, then chain them like an assembly line: make the text shout, add exclamation marks, and repeat a chant.
why: String functions show how to transform text step by step. Chaining small functions is how real programs build formatted messages, reports, and UI labels.
analogy: String formatting is like a photo editing app with filters. You apply the uppercase filter, then the add-excitement filter, then the repeat filter. Each filter transforms the string and hands it to the next one.
try_it: Add a `whisper(text: Str) -> Str` function using `string.str_lower`, then print both the shout and whisper versions of the headline.
tips: `string.str_upper(text)` takes one `Str` and returns a new `Str`; it does not change the original.
`string.str_concat(a, b)` takes exactly two `Str` values and returns their join. For three pieces, nest calls or use `+`.
Every function that promises `-> Str` must return a `Str` on every path; a while loop alone does not return a value.
Build a pipeline by storing each function's result in a new variable before passing it on.
common_mistakes: Forgetting `return result;` in `repeat_word` - the function promises a `Str`, so the compiler needs a returned value.
Passing three arguments to `string.str_concat`; it takes exactly two.
Forgetting spaces in the pieces: `string.str_concat("Go!", "Go!")` gives `Go!Go!`.
